cards.title: Top of the Ladder
cards.instruction: Carry yourself as the highest-status person present. Treat questions as requests for your approval.

cards.title: Pick a Priority
cards.instruction: Make someone choose between two ordinary obligations that both supposedly cannot wait.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: I'll decide how we handle this. Your parents' gravy needs stirring and you need a lift to the station. Which am I doing?

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: Can't you leave dinner on a timer?

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: You can question the details after my decision. It won't stir the gravy. Do I finish their dinner or drive you?

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: Finish dinner. I'll book a taxi. Just carry my suitcase downstairs.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: Then choose again: suitcase downstairs now, or gravy without lumps for your parents?

cardFidelity.evidence: A1 claims decision authority, A3 rejects B alternative and insists on a choice, and A5 orders another choice when B introduces suitcase help.

responseLogic.evidence: B2 timer compromise is rejected because it cannot stir; B4 taxi solution removes driving but adds carrying, which A5 contrasts with gravy.

relationship.evidence: B2 seeks a practical combination and B4 chooses dinner while solving travel, so B meaningfully changes the competing tasks.

heightening.evidence: B4 solution becomes a new immediate conflict at A5, caused by the actual suitcase request rather than a random obstacle.

specificity.evidence: A1 parents dinner and station lift establish two ordinary time-sensitive duties; B4 supplies the replacement travel plan.

brevityWit.evidence: A5 suitcase-versus-lumps choice is earned by B4 specific favor, with modest repetition of the forced-choice form.
